chunks: "The difference is whether the inductor current ever hits zero.
In continuous conduction, CCM, the current ramps up during the on-time and down during the off-time but never reaches zero, so there are two states per cycle.

In discontinuous conduction, DCM, the current falls to zero before the cycle ends, and for the rest of the period both switches are effectively off and the inductor current sits at zero, so there are three states.
Which one you're in depends on load. The ripple current is fixed by V in , V out , L and frequency, so as the load drops the average falls and eventually the valley touches zero.
That boundary is at I out equals change in I L over 2 . For my usual 12-to-3. 3 volts, 4. 7 microhenries, 500 kilohertz example that's about half an amp.
The big consequence is the gain. In CCM, V out equals D V in regardless of load, so the loop has an easy job.
In DCM the same duty cycle gives a higher output, and it rises as load falls, so the controller has to cut the duty cycle as the load drops.
You also get higher peak current for the same average, ringing at the switch node during the idle time, and a different small-signal response, closer to a single pole.

On the plus side, DCM turns on at zero current, so there's no reverse recovery loss, and at light load it's much more efficient if the low-side FET turns off at zero current, since it avoids circulating ripple current."
